demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Fadi Mansour was seventy-eight when the accident happened. He had spent fifty-two years as an environmental scientist, the last thirty-five at a consulting firm where he was known for his meticulous attention to detail and his quiet, methodical way of solving problems. His colleagues respected him. His wife, Layla, whom he had married in Damascus before immigrating to California in 1975, had grown accustomed to his long silences-they were the silences of a man thinking, not a man troubled. Or so she had believed.

The incident occurred on a Saturday morning in October at the community garden where Fadi and Layla volunteered. Fadi had been helping an elderly neighbor, Mrs. Chen, move a heavy wooden planter box. She was frail, in her mid-eighties, and he had done this work many times before. But that morning, as they both lifted, his foot caught on an uneven stone. He fell forward. The planter-filled with soil and stone, weighing perhaps eighty pounds-came down across her left leg. She screamed. The sound was immediate and terrible. When the paramedics arrived, they told him her femur was fractured in three places. She would need surgery. She would be in the hospital for weeks.

Fadi had apologized profusely. Mrs. Chen, from her hospital bed, had told him it was an accident. Layla had held his hand and said the same thing. But something in Fadi had fractured too, in a way that no surgery could repair. For the first few weeks, he could not sleep. When he closed his eyes, he was back in that moment-Mrs. Chen's weight shifting, his own body falling, the sickening impact of stone on bone. But the strangest part was that when he tried to speak about it to Layla, the words simply would not come. He knew what had happened. He could see it, frame by frame, as if watching a film. But when he opened his mouth, nothing emerged that felt adequate or even real. He would start: "I was holding the-" and then stop, frustrated. The event felt too extreme, too impossible. Had it really happened that way? Had the sound really been so loud? Had Mrs. Chen's cry really lasted so long? His mind kept rejecting the memory as though it were a lie he had invented.

Three months into his suffering, Fadi began to notice that certain sounds made him acutely afraid. Heavy breathing-the kind Layla made when she was relaxed on the sofa in the evening, or the sound of his own breath when he exerted himself-triggered a panic that felt like drowning. He realized, though he could not articulate it clearly, that it was the sound of life continuing, of ease, while he carried this weight. But the breathing was only part of it. What truly unsettled him was when he found himself in moments of contentment-rare as they had become. One afternoon, sitting in his study with afternoon light falling through the window, he had felt a brief, unexpected lightness. For just a few seconds, he had almost smiled. Then the feeling deepened into something like happiness, a small warmth in his chest, and immediately his body seized with terror. How could he be happy? How could he allow himself to feel relaxed or at ease when Mrs. Chen was still in physical therapy, still struggling to walk? The moment he recognized the happiness, it turned toxic. His chest tightened. His mind flooded with images of her screaming. He had come to believe that any moment of his own peace was a betrayal-a sign that he was forgetting, that he was letting himself off too easily. So he learned to notice happiness the moment it began to bloom and to crush it before it could take root. He would stand abruptly, find something to worry about, remind himself of what he had done. When Layla tried to embrace him one evening, reaching for him as she always did, he stiffened. Her arms around him felt like a trap. He could not bear the tenderness. It made no sense to him; he loved his wife. But affection felt dangerous now, as if kindness were a delusion he could no longer afford.

He began to withdraw from work. He took early retirement, citing age and fatigue, though his colleagues were surprised-Fadi had seemed vital just months before. At home, he spent long hours in his study, ostensibly reading, but mostly sitting in silence. He avoided the community garden entirely. He began making excuses not to see his grandchildren. When they visited, he would retreat to another room. Layla grew worried. She asked him repeatedly if he was unwell, if he needed to see a doctor. He could not explain to her that what was wrong with him had no medical name, or rather, that it had a name but the name itself felt like an insult to the woman whose leg he had broken. It was Layla who finally insisted he see someone. She had noticed him becoming smaller, more absent, as if he were disappearing into the guilt. She made the appointment herself. Fadi came to the first session reluctant and ashamed, carrying the memory of Mrs. Chen like a stone he could neither put down nor speak aloud.

missing.item: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed (as a trigger)
missing.explanation: While the vignette mentions Layla being 'relaxed on the sofa in the evening,' this is used as context for the breathing sound trigger, not as an independent trigger of feeling happy or relaxed itself. The patient reported that 'feeling happy or relaxed' is a trigger for PTSD symptoms, but the vignette does not show Fadi experiencing distress specifically when he himself feels happy or relaxed—only when exposed to auditory cues (heavy breathing) or affection. The trigger item 'Feeling Happy' as a distinct phenomenological experience is not demonstrated in the vignette.
